vignette:
He is a 55-year-old man from Oceania who now works as a nanny, though he does not introduce himself that way at first. When he talks about himself, he starts with his family. He says he has always been the one who watches, who notices when someone is tired before they say so, who wakes easily to small sounds in the night. Those qualities once made him a dependable husband and father, and now they make him good with children. But when he tells the story of how his life changed, he returns again and again to the day his younger sister was badly injured.

At the time, he is still married and working irregular caregiving jobs while helping his extended family whenever he can. His sister is someone he feels responsible for, even though she is an adult. She calls him often, and he prides himself on being available. On the day of the trauma, he misses her call. He is in the shower, then driving, then thinking he will ring her back after he finishes an errand. Before he can, another family member calls to say there has been a violent incident and she is in the hospital. He remembers the drive there in fragments: gripping the steering wheel too tightly, feeling certain he will be too late, hearing the phone buzz and being unable to answer.

In the emergency department, he sees her on a bed surrounded by noise, bright light, and strangers moving quickly. He does not go into graphic detail, but he remembers the unnatural stillness of her face and the sound of machines around her. He keeps thinking she might die before he can speak to her. He says that in those first hours, something in him "freezes and burns at the same time." He feels unreal, as if he is watching another family go through it. At the same time, he is intensely alert. He notices the blood on a nurse's glove, the smell of disinfectant, the squeak of shoes on the floor. Later, these become the details that return to him uninvited.

His sister survives, but the event does not end when she leaves the hospital. For months he is at appointments, helping with meals, fielding calls from relatives, trying to be steady. Outwardly he functions. Inwardly he keeps replaying the missed phone call and the image of her in the hospital bed. He lies awake imagining different versions of that day in which he answers immediately, arrives sooner, prevents everything. He knows, rationally, that he did not cause what happened, but the thought does not loosen its hold. Guilt becomes a private ritual. He revisits it nightly.

Over time his marriage deteriorates. He describes becoming "hard to live with." He startles when someone comes up behind him. He scans rooms for exits without meaning to. If a loved one is late, he calls repeatedly, then becomes angry at himself for sounding panicked. His ex-wife tells him he is physically present but never relaxed, never really home. He sleeps in brief stretches and wakes sweating from dreams in which hospital alarms are sounding or his phone rings and he cannot reach it. Some nights he stays up until dawn because sleep feels like losing control.

His work as a nanny suits and strains him in equal measure. Children respond to his gentleness, and he likes the practical rhythm of packing lunches, walking to school, kneeling to tie shoes, remembering who likes the crusts cut off. Caring for them gives him structure and a reason to keep moving. But the job also keeps him close to the very fear that now organizes his life. At the playground he cannot sit on the bench the way other caregivers do. He circles constantly, eyes on the gate, the road, the climbing frame. If one child disappears behind a slide for even a second, his heart lurches and his mind jumps to catastrophe. He masks it by sounding cheerful-"Stay where I can see you, mate"-but inside he is already back in the hospital corridor.

He avoids certain things without fully admitting that he is avoiding them. He takes different routes so he does not pass the hospital. He silences unknown numbers because sudden calls make his chest tighten. Family gatherings have become complicated; everyone expects him to be the reliable one, but conversations about his sister's recovery make him detach. He nods, gets tea, changes the subject. He says he feels ashamed that others seem to have "moved on" while he is still ambushed by memories.

Now, years later, he lives alone after the divorce. His flat is neat, almost spare. He keeps his phone charged and within reach at all times. He checks on people too much, then apologizes for checking. He describes feeling tired in a way sleep does not fix. There are moments of closeness with the children he cares for-reading stories on the sofa, hearing them laugh in the back seat, watching them run to a parent at pickup-that bring warmth and also a sharp, immediate fear of how quickly safety can vanish. He knows this reaction is larger than the present moment, but knowing does not stop it.

When he speaks about his sister now, his voice softens. She is alive, and he is grateful. Yet the event remains unfinished inside him. He still lives as if the next phone call could change everything.
